summary.text: A 14-month-old male neutered domestic shorthair cat presented to an emergency clinic with generalized tremors, anorexia and lethargy; bloodwork showed elevated globulins and a decreased albumin-globulin ratio and the FIP 7B ELISA was high, prompting a presumptive diagnosis of FIP. He received a prednisolone taper and owner-sourced GS-441524 injections, then became ataxic and was referred to neurology.

Neurology examination showed a left sided head tilt, vestibular ataxia and decreased postural reactions. MRI showed hydrocephalus and inflammatory changes consistent with neurologic FIP; CSF analysis was not performed. The 84-day GS-441524 course was completed without complications and a follow-up exam 1 month later showed resolved head tilt with mild residual deficits.

He was re-presented with vestibular signs; repeat MRI showed markedly progressive hydrocephalus without evidence of active inflammation. A Codman programmable ventriculoperitoneal shunt was placed in the right lateral ventricle, CSF cytology showed no inflammation and FCoV PCR was negative.

He was discharged 2 days after shunt placement, re-evaluated at 2 weeks and 3 months with only mild or equivocal vestibular ataxia, and was doing well at home 1 year after shunt placement and alive at the time of writing.

summary.text: A 14-month-old male neutered domestic shorthair cat presented to neurology with episodes of non-distractable self-mutilation and aggression; complex partial seizures were suspected and phenobarbital improved the episodes. After 2 months he was re-presented with behavior changes and ataxia, with obtundation, nystagmus and decreased left postural reactions.

Brain MRI showed hydrocephalus and ependymal enhancement consistent with FIP. He received dexamethasone and then GS-441524 injections for 50 days followed by oral capsules for 34 days, and at the end of treatment he showed left-sided vestibular ataxia but could walk without support.

He was re-presented 14 months post treatment with difficulty walking and marked progression of hydrocephalus on MRI. A shunt was initially declined, a urinary obstruction occurred, and a programmable VPS was later placed in the left ventricle with later pressure reductions that improved mobility.

After further urinary obstruction and cystotomy he was humanely euthanized for complete urinary obstruction. Necropsy showed no active FIP infection and negative FIP IHC; the ventricular necropsy findings are described inconsistently in the source.

summary.text: A 10-month-old male neutered Maine Coone cat presented with lethargy and ataxia that had progressed despite a week of prednisolone. Examination showed a non-ambulatory cat with thoracic limb extensor rigidity and minimal motor function, with episodes of opisthotonus; brain MRI showed diffuse ventriculomegaly and meningeal enhancement consistent with FIP.
He received an 84-day course of GS-441524 injections at 10 mg/kg/day with a prednisolone taper, and his neurological exam was normal 2 weeks after finishing the injections.

At 26 months old he presented through the emergency department for concern of FIP recurrence with a week-long progressive vestibular ataxia, was given a single GS-441524 dose, and repeat MRI showed progressive hydrocephalus with cerebellar herniation; CSF was not collected. Medical management with dexamethasone and omeprazole was followed by decline when the dexamethasone was tapered.

At 3 months post diagnosis he had declined and a 100 cm H2O Codman fixed pressure VPS was placed in the left lateral ventricle; he could ambulate independently the day after surgery, was neurologically normal apart from mildly delayed right thoracic limb postural reactions at 2 weeks, and was doing well at home 8 months post-operatively.

summary.text: A 7-month-old female spayed domestic shorthair cat presented with progressive pelvic limb ataxia over 2 to 3 weeks and was ataxic in the pelvic limbs without postural deficits. Thoracolumbar spine MRI was unremarkable, sagittal brain scans were abnormal, and brain MRI showed diffuse ventriculomegaly with periventricular hyperintensity consistent with FIP.
She received prednisolone tapering over 2 weeks and GS-441524 injections at 10 mg/kg for 84 days, and was re-evaluated 2 weeks after finishing the GS course with a normal neurologic exam.

She was presented again 15 months later for yearly monitoring, clinically normal at home with an unremarkable neurological exam. Recheck MRI showed mildly improved ventriculomegaly, CSF cytology and fluid analysis were unremarkable and FCoV PCR on spinal fluid was negative; the discussion notes no progressive neurologic signs and no discernible fourth ventricle enlargement.

article_limitations: Each narrative paragraph sits under its literal "Case 1" to "Case 4 (control)" heading (segment heading field and article XML), so the case-to-cat mapping is literal; the headings are not repeated in the segment text. Patients are numbered by the case narratives (Cats 1-4) although the abstract and introduction mention Cat 2 and Case 4 earlier; those mentions refer to the labelled cases.
The text cites Supplementary Image 1 and Supplementary Image 2; the source lists no supplements, so these images were not available.

Table 1 cells carry no explicit time except through row labels (Initial, Recheck, Re-check, Post VPS). Narrative statements that cite Table 1 for the same finding (Cat 1 bloodwork and ELISA; Cat 2 initial examination) are one item citing both; other narrative statements are not linked to table cells.

Table 2 row suffixes a and b are not defined inside Table 2; the figure captions use a and b for the FIP diagnosis or initial MRI and for re-presentation or the repeat MRI, but no time was assigned to Table 2 values.

Cat 2 necropsy ventricular findings conflict between Table 1 and the abstract (marked dilation, moderate to severe hydrocephalus) and the discussion (ventricular system unremarkable); both are kept as review_only source_conflict facts.
Re-presentation intervals differ between Table 1 (months from diagnosis) and the narrative (months post treatment or later) for all cats; the anchors differ and no single interval was derived.
NA entries in Table 1 are not defined in the footnote and are kept as ambiguous review_only observations.

Cohort-level discussion statements (none of the cats experienced relapse, all cats responded to VPS, all cats showing vestibular signs had resolution of ventriculitis) were not copied to individual cats.
Table 2 Cat 2b left ventricle ratio (36.73%) does not equal the ratio computed from its printed heights (about 36.9%); arithmetic only.
